title: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Login Hook
shortTitle: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Login Hook
summary: A login hook is a macOS preference setting that names a script to run automatically whenever a user logs in, and a logout hook does the same at logoff. The setting lives in the com.apple.loginwindow property list and can be edited with the defaults command, but changing it requires administrator rights. Because the hook script runs with root privileges, an adversary who can write to that file converts a single line of configuration into command execution with the highest available privilege, repeated at every login. There can only be one login hook and one logout hook on a system at a time, so an intruder either adds their own hook or appends commands to an existing one, which often means quietly editing a script the administrator already trusts. Defenders distinguish this from legitimate use by checking whether the named script exists, who owns it, and how recently the property list changed; on modern macOS the mechanism is deprecated in favour of launch agents and launch daemons, so any hook at all is worth explaining. Relevant artefacts include the property list file itself, its modification timestamps, the hook script on disk, and the parent-child process chain that appears at each logon.

beginner.definition: This is a macOS setting that says which script the computer must run each time somebody logs in. It is stored in a system settings file and it runs with full administrator power. An attacker who can change that setting can run their own code with the same power.
beginner.whyItMatters: The script runs as root, which is the most powerful account on the machine. That means one small settings change can give an intruder complete control. It also runs again at every single login, so the access does not stop after a restart. Few people look at this setting, so it can stay hidden for a long time.
howItWorks: At login the system reads a settings file called com.apple.loginwindow for a value named LoginHook.
That value holds the path of a script, and the system starts the script with root privileges.
An attacker with administrator rights adds or changes the value using the defaults command.
The named script might be a brand new file or an existing trusted script that now has extra lines.
Only one login hook and one logout hook can exist at a time, so old ones are replaced or edited.
At the next login the script runs again, which keeps the attacker present without any user action.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel front desk with a printed instruction card taped inside the drawer. It says that whenever a guest checks in, staff must unlock the safe and follow the note inside. Only the manager may replace that card. If someone swaps the card for one naming a different note, every single check-in quietly follows the new instruction instead. The staff did nothing wrong and noticed nothing unusual, because they only ever read the official card.
takeaways: A login hook is a settings entry that starts a script as root at every login.
Because the script runs as root, changing it is as serious as giving away the administrator password.
Check this setting against a known good baseline, and treat any unexpected change as suspicious.

objectives: Explain what a login hook is and why it runs with root privileges.
Describe how the com.apple.loginwindow property list and the defaults command relate to logon execution.
Identify the file and process artefacts a defender can use to review login hook changes.
Distinguish an intentional login hook from an adversary modification on a managed Mac.
Summarise why this macOS mechanism was replaced by launch agents and launch daemons.
